description: السلام عليكم، أنا فارس آل خضر (17 سنة)، سأبني مشروعاً تقنياً متكاملاً لـ NASA Space Apps يدمج الذكاء الاصطناعي وإنترنت الأشياء لحل تحديات الفضاء.ابحث عن شركاء مبدعين في تصميم  العروض التقديمية، سرد القصة (Storytelling)، والتقديم أمام لجان التحكيم. إذا عندك شغف، حياك معنا
summary: AstroHab is a crew health monitoring system for long space missions. It reads live vital signs (heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, radiation, stress, bone density), adds crew self check-ins (blood pressure, glucose, sleep, mood), and compares every reading with limits taken only from NASA or named US-government sources. Each alarm shows where its limit came from. Alerts reach the crew through a live dashboard with an interactive body map, a physical buzzer on an ESP32 board, a bilingual (Arabic/English) AI assistant, and a PDF summary for flight surgeons. The assistant uses Gemini when online and switches automatically to a local assistant when the connection drops, so the crew always gets an answer. NASA data is the core of the project. We processed ECG recordings from NASA’s Crew State Monitoring dataset (17 subjects, 1,546 windows) and derived the heart-rate warning limit of 83 bpm (95th percentile). Danger limits come from NASA-STD-3001 and OCHMO-STD-100.1A. It matters because crews far from Earth must catch health problems on board, with alarms that are traceable and never invented.
details: WHAT IT DOES: AstroHab turns live crew vitals into alerts that always cite a source. A rules engine compares each reading with a warning and a danger limit and reports Stable, Warning or Danger. Limits are loaded from one file (limits.csv) where every row carries its NASA or US-government source; no limit is hard-coded, and a metric without a limit shows “limits not set” instead of a guess. The system also tracks trends with an early warning and a cumulative radiation dose against NASA’s 600 mSv limit. HOW IT WORKS: (1) NASA ECG recordings (256 Hz) are band-pass filtered (5-25 Hz), R-peaks are detected, and heart rate is computed in 30-second windows. The 95th percentile of 1,546 valid windows from 17 subjects gives the 83 bpm warning limit. (2) Danger limits come from NASA OCHMO-STD-100.1A (heart rate above 130 or below 30), bone density from NASA-STD-3001 (V1 4027) and radiation from V1 4030. Where NASA publishes no limit (blood oxygen, glucose, temperature, blood pressure crisis), we use named US-government sources (MedlinePlus, NIDDK, NHLBI), labelled as such in the app. (3) Outputs: live dashboard with an interactive body map, a physical buzzer on an ESP32 board (fail-safe if the link drops), a voice assistant in Arabic and English, and a PDF/CSV summary for flight surgeons. (4) The assistant answers with Gemini when online and with a local rule-based assistant when offline, using the same live data. It never diagnoses and never invents readings. IMPACT: Crews far from Earth cannot wait for ground support, so AstroHab gives them early, explainable warnings on board. The same approach can serve remote clinics on Earth. TOOLS: Python, Flask, SQLite, numpy/scipy, reportlab, Chart.js, XIAO ESP32-C5 with buzzer and button, Google Gemini API, 190 automated tests. CREATIVITY: Every alarm shows the source of its limit, and one derived limit is computed from NASA recordings rather than copied. LIMITATIONS: Readings in the demo are simulated. The NASA recordings come from a small sample of simulator tasks, so the 83 bpm limit needs validation on more data. Sleep, stress and mood have no published NASA limits yet. The method for the 83 bpm limit is explained in RESOURCES.md in the repository. SI ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: The code, tests, documentation and presentation of AstroHab were developed with the assistance of Claude (Anthropic). The in-app assistant uses Google Gemini at run time. All screenshots are captured from the running application; no images or videos were generated by SI.
